passage:
School photo day, and the queue outside the library moved slowly. When Madhuri's turn came, she climbed onto the stool and stretched her mouth into a huge grin, every tooth showing, eyebrows up, eyes not smiling at all.

"Lovely! Hold it!" said the photographer.

Afterwards, Himani Ma'am knelt beside her. "Your cheeks must be tired."

"I didn't feel like smiling," Madhuri whispered. "My tooth is wobbly."

"That's all right. A photo smile is just a photo smile. You don't have to feel it."

qa.q: Where was the queue for school photos?
qa.a: Outside the library.

qa.q: What was Madhuri feeling behind her big grin?
qa.a: She was probably uncomfortable and not very happy, since her tooth was wobbly and her eyes were not smiling. She may also have been a bit shy on the stool in front of everyone.

qa.q: How did Himani Ma'am support Madhuri after the photo?
qa.a: She noticed the stiff grin, asked gently, and told Madhuri a photo smile does not have to match how she feels, so there was no pressure to be happy. 🙂

qa.q: How does the photographer see Madhuri's smile?
qa.a: The photographer only sees a cheerful, toothy grin and says "Lovely!", without noticing the tired, unsmiling eyes.

grounding: It shows a preschooler's stiff, toothy smile on cue for a photo and an adult accepting it without insisting she feel happy.

passage:
The clinic waiting room was crowded and quiet. Varun, holding his father's hand, spotted a girl on the next bench with a toy car. He raised his eyebrows at her, quick, up and down, and grinned.

Sarika didn't notice. She was busy rolling the car along her mother's knee.

Varun tried again. Eyebrows up, down. Nothing.

His father leaned over. "Maybe say it with words too."

Varun slid off the bench. "Hi! Can I race your car?"

Sarika looked up and held it out.

qa.q: What was Sarika rolling the toy car along?
qa.a: Her mother's knee.

qa.q: What did Varun want when he flashed his eyebrows at Sarika?
qa.a: He was most likely feeling friendly and eager to play, using the eyebrow flash as a quick hello. Another reading is that he was just curious about the toy car.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Saying "Hi! Can I race your car?" worked because the quick eyebrow signal was easy to miss, and the words made his invitation clear.

qa.q: What is it like for Sarika when Varun first raises his eyebrows?
qa.a: She doesn't notice at all, because she is busy with her car, so to her nothing has happened yet.

grounding: It shows a child flashing his eyebrows as a quick hello and invitation, and a spoken greeting making it clear when the signal is missed.

passage:
In the back garden in Leeds, Chen crouched over Nadia's bike, trying to get the chain back on. His eyebrows pulled low and close together, and he didn't say a word.

Nadia stopped bouncing her ball. She stood very still, then whispered, "Sorry, Baba."

Chen looked up, surprised. "Sorry for what?"

"You're cross."

"Oh!" He laughed and wiped his oily fingers. "No, sweetheart. This is my thinking face. The chain is tricky. I'm not cross with you at all."

Nadia came closer to watch.

qa.q: What was Chen trying to put back on Nadia's bike?
qa.a: The chain.

qa.q: Why did Nadia stop bouncing her ball and say sorry?
qa.a: She read Chen's low, drawn-together eyebrows as crossness and felt worried that she had done something wrong. She may also have felt uneasy because he had gone silent.

qa.q: What did Chen do that helped Nadia?
qa.a: He told her plainly that it was his thinking face and he was not cross, so she learnt the same look can mean concentrating.

qa.q: How does Chen see the moment when Nadia apologises?
qa.a: He is surprised, because he was only concentrating on the chain and had no idea his face looked angry to her.

grounding: It shows a preschooler reading drawn-together eyebrows as anger and going quiet, then being told it was concentration.

subtype: Eyes shut against a scary scene [Regulating]
passage:
I'm Manjula, and I was sitting on the floor next to my little brother Anand for film night. Amma had picked a jungle cartoon.

When the crocodile crept up out of the river, Anand squeezed his eyes tight shut and pressed both hands over his face. He peeked once through his fingers, then shut them again.

I held out my hand and he grabbed it. Amma pressed pause. "Want a break, kanna?"

He shook his head, still hiding. When the music turned happy, he opened his eyes.

qa.q: What crept up out of the river in the film?
qa.a: The crocodile crept up out of the river.

qa.q: What was Anand probably feeling when he squeezed his eyes shut?
qa.a: He was most likely scared of the crocodile and hid his eyes to handle the fear. Peeking through his fingers suggests he was also curious to see what happened.

qa.q: How did Amma and Manjula help Anand cope?
qa.a: Manjula offered a hand to hold and Amma paused the film and offered a break, letting Anand choose how to manage.

qa.q: What would change if someone had laughed at Anand for hiding?
qa.a: He might have felt ashamed of a healthy way of coping and could have stopped showing when he was frightened.

grounding: It shows a child shutting his eyes during a frightening film scene to manage fear, with family offering a hand and a break.

passage:
Before the painting class at the community centre, Maria and Preeti had hidden a paper flower in Teacher's drawer.

When Teacher sat down, Maria looked across at Preeti and tried to wink. Both her eyes squeezed shut together, and her whole nose wrinkled.

Preeti clapped a hand over her mouth to stop a giggle. She knew exactly what the double blink meant.

Teacher opened the drawer. "Oh! Who did this?"

Maria tried to wink again. Both eyes. Preeti snorted. 😆

qa.q: What had Maria and Preeti hidden in Teacher's drawer?
qa.a: A paper flower.

qa.q: What was Preeti feeling when she clapped a hand over her mouth?
qa.a: She was most likely amused and excited, trying not to give away the secret. She might also have been a little nervous that Teacher would guess.

qa.q: What makes Maria's wink work even though both eyes shut?
qa.a: The two friends share the secret, so Preeti understands the playful signal even when the wink is clumsy.

qa.q: How might Teacher see the two girls' giggling?
qa.a: Teacher might guess from the blinking and snorting that they share a joke and are behind the flower.

grounding: It shows a preschooler blinking both eyes while trying to wink about a shared secret, which her friend still understands.

passage:
Monday: Lavanya had drawn on the wall with crayons. "Look at me when I'm talking to you!" Aditi said sharply. Lavanya stared harder at her toes. Her chin trembled and she said nothing.

Wednesday: juice on the sofa. This time Aditi sat down beside her and spoke softly. "The sofa is sticky now. What can we do?" Lavanya kept her eyes down for a while, then looked up. "Get a cloth?"

Saturday: Lavanya came running. "Mama, I spilled water. I'll get the cloth!"

qa.q: What did Lavanya draw on the wall with?
qa.a: Crayons.

qa.q: Why did Lavanya stare at her toes on Monday?
qa.a: She was probably ashamed and scared of being told off, and looking down was a way to avoid more upset. Her trembling chin suggests she was close to tears.

qa.q: What changed on Wednesday that helped?
qa.a: Aditi sat beside her, used a soft voice and did not demand eye contact, so Lavanya felt safe enough to look up and suggest getting a cloth.

qa.q: What is it like for Aditi by Saturday?
qa.a: It is likely a relief for her: Lavanya now comes to tell her about a spill herself instead of hiding it.

grounding: It shows a preschooler looking down when scolded and a calm, gentle approach working better than demanding eye contact.

passage:
The temple fair in the village was crowded, but Tanuja only had eyes for one person: a visitor with bright blue hair and a big camera. Tanuja stared, mouth open, and trailed after her from the bangle stall to the swings.

The visitor turned, caught Tanuja staring again, and shifted her camera bag, looking unsure.

Jahnavi Didi crouched beside her sister. "Blue hair is new for you, na? But when someone keeps staring, it can feel odd. Try smiling and saying namaste."

Tanuja smiled. The visitor smiled back.

qa.q: What colour was the visitor's hair?
qa.a: Bright blue.

qa.q: Why did Tanuja keep staring and following the visitor?
qa.a: She was most likely curious and fascinated by the blue hair, something she had never seen. She may also have been drawn to the big camera.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi Didi handle the staring?
qa.a: She explained kindly why staring can feel odd and gave Tanuja something friendly to do instead, without shaming her.

qa.q: How does the visitor feel when Tanuja keeps staring?
qa.a: The visitor seems uneasy, shifting the camera bag and looking unsure, until Tanuja's smile turns it into a friendly moment.

grounding: It shows a young child staring at an unusual sight out of curiosity and an older sister kindly explaining how staring can feel to others.

passage:
On the verandah of their small-town house, Trisha cut the last mango and said, "That's all for today."

Mahima puffed out her cheeks like two balloons, crossed her eyes and let out a loud "Hmph!" Then she peeked at her cousin and giggled. Trisha puffed her cheeks back, and they both laughed.

That evening, when Trisha switched off the cartoons, Mahima puffed her cheeks again. This time she turned her back, arms folded, and stamped into the other room without a sound.

qa.q: What did Trisha cut on the verandah?
qa.a: The last mango.

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling the second time she puffed her cheeks?
qa.a: She was probably truly irritated about the cartoons being switched off; turning her back, folding her arms and stamping away show real annoyance. She may also have been tired by evening.

qa.q: How could Trisha tell the two cheek puffs apart?
qa.a: By watching the rest of Mahima: giggling and peeking meant theatre, while a turned back, folded arms and silence meant real crossness.

qa.q: What would change if Trisha treated both puffs as a joke?
qa.a: She might tease Mahima when she was really upset, and Mahima could feel laughed at instead of understood.

grounding: It shows the same cheek puff as comic theatre in one moment and real irritation in another, with the body showing which.

passage:
Rain hammered the car roof and the traffic had not moved for ten minutes. School started soon. Eshaan gripped the wheel, jaw tight, nostrils flaring with each breath.

In the back seat, Mohit stopped kicking his feet. "Papa, your nose is doing the angry thing."

Eshaan caught his eye in the mirror and let out a breath. "You're right. I'm feeling cross at the traffic, not at you. Let's slow down together." He breathed in slowly. Mohit copied him, puffing his cheeks. 🙂

qa.q: How long had the traffic not moved?
qa.a: Ten minutes.

qa.q: What was Mohit feeling when he stopped kicking his feet?
qa.a: He was likely uneasy and a little worried, because he had sensed tension in Papa's flaring nostrils. He may also just have been curious about the face Papa was making.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Eshaan named the feeling calmly and said it was about the traffic, not Mohit, then showed slow breathing, which eased the tension for both.

qa.q: How does Eshaan see the moment when Mohit points out his nose?
qa.a: He is caught off guard, but he takes the comment seriously and uses it as a chance to calm himself down.

grounding: It shows a child noticing an adult's flaring nostrils as a sign of anger and the adult naming the feeling and modelling slowing down.

subtype: Biting a lip and licking lips [Mismatch]
passage:
The sack race at the village sports day was next. Divyansh stood at the start line in the hot sun, licking his lips again and again, then biting his lower lip hard.

"He's scared," his cousin Dhruv told Dadi.

"Maybe," said Dadi. "Or thirsty. He's been out here all morning." She handed Divyansh the water bottle. He gulped half of it.

Still, when the whistle-man raised his arm, Divyansh bit his lip again and stared straight at the finish flag.

qa.q: What race was next at the village sports day?
qa.a: The sack race.

qa.q: What might Divyansh be feeling when he bites his lip as the whistle-man raises his arm?
qa.a: After drinking water he still bites his lip, so he may be nervous about the race or concentrating hard on the finish flag; thirst alone no longer explains it.

qa.q: What did Dadi do well before guessing?
qa.a: She checked the setting, the hot sun and a long morning outside, and offered water before deciding what the lip-licking meant.

qa.q: Why might Dhruv read the lip-biting differently from Dadi?
qa.a: Dhruv jumped to "scared" from the lip-biting alone, while Dadi thought about the heat and saw that thirst was also possible.

grounding: It shows a child licking and biting his lips before a race, with the cause possibly thirst, nerves or concentration.
